chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A man invited one of the Banu Hashim to single combat (mubarazah), but he refused to accept. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) asked him, 'What prevented you from accepting?' He said, 'He was the horseman of the Arabs, and I feared he would kill me.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Indeed, he is aggressive towards you; if you had accepted, you would have killed him. And if a mountain were aggressive towards a mountain, the aggressor would be toppled.'

And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) invited a man to single combat. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) learned of this and said to him,

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Title for Imam Ali)
key_terms.فَارِسَ الْعَرَبِ: The horseman of the Arabs (referring to skill in battle)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on single combat (mubarazah) and the etiquette of accepting challenges?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith elucidates the jurisprudential and ethical nuances of *mubarazah* (single combat) within the Shia tradition. It establishes that the initiator of the challenge (*al-baghi*) bears the burden of proof and is destined for defeat, thereby removing the excuse of fear for the challenger, while also emphasizing the necessity of consistent conduct (*istiqamah*) in personal interactions to maintain dignity.
